author: Rahul kp
title: Capital vs Revenue
hook: benefit for years, or just this year?
simple_words: Spending that gives benefit for many years is capital; spending that is used up this year is revenue.

definitions.meaning: Spending that acquires or improves a fixed asset or increases earning capacity, with benefit beyond one year. Shown in the Balance Sheet.
Spending to run the business and maintain earning capacity, with benefit used up in the current year. Charged to Trading or P&L Account.

key_points: Capital expenditure adds to the ==cost of an asset==, including freight, installation and erection charges.
Revenue expenditure covers repairs, wages, rent, salaries and depreciation.
!!Wrongly treating capital as revenue understates profit and assets!!; the reverse overstates profit.
Test: does it create or improve an asset's life or capacity, or only maintain it?

insight.text: Buying a machine is capital, but ordinary repairs on it are revenue; the purpose of spending decides the class.

memory_trick.explanation: If the spending is cemented into the asset (buy, install, extend, improve), it is capital. If it only keeps the asset running (repair, paint, oil), it is revenue.

steps: Read what the payment was for
Does it add or improve the asset?
Yes: capitalise, add to asset cost
No: charge to P&L or Trading A/c
exam_tip: !!Freight, installation and legal fees on buying an asset are capital!!; ordinary repairs and renewals to maintain it are revenue.

doubt.question: Is a repair always revenue?
doubt.answer: No. Repairs at purchase to make a second-hand asset usable are capital. Ordinary repairs that only maintain the asset are revenue.

mistakes.wrong: Treating wages paid for installing a new machine as revenue
mistakes.right: Wages for installing a new machine are capital and added to the machine's cost.
Repairs to make a newly bought second-hand asset fit for use are capital.

mistakes.wrong: Charging the purchase of furniture to Purchases A/c
mistakes.right: Furniture is a fixed asset, so it is capital and goes to Furniture A/c.
Nature and purpose decide, not size; a large repair bill to maintain an asset is still revenue.

check_notes: Checker 1: Key point 4 (wording only): 'does it create or improve an asset's life or capacity' is awkward. Better: 'Test: does it acquire an asset or increase its life or earning capacity (capital), or only maintain it (revenue)?'

Checker 2: Key point 2: depreciation is a non-cash charge, not an outlay of money. It is better to say 'revenue expenses such as repairs, wages, rent and salaries, and depreciation is charged to P&L'. This is wording only.

Checker 2: Exam tip: 'renewals' could mislead. Only minor or ordinary replacements are revenue. Replacing a major part that extends the asset's life or capacity is capital. Say 'ordinary repairs and minor replacements'. This is wording only.
